extracted.intended_audience: general readers; students and researchers in media and fandom studies
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize the characteristics, behaviors, community forms, and harms associated with anti-fans/anti-fandom for readers studying or encountering anti-fan activity. The page describes definitions, typical behaviors (hate-watching, snark), group dynamics, extreme examples, and topics studied by scholars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of anti-fan / hater
rubrics_metrics.description: An anti-fan (also called a hater, toxic fan, detractor or anti) is someone who enjoys writing, discussing, or (in some cases) making derivative works about a piece of media, but solely for the purpose of railing against or parodying it. It can also be a person with hatred towards a celebrity or icon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the core identifying criterion: participation with the media or celebrity is motivated primarily by dislike, hostility, parody, or ridicule rather than appreciation or neutral critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose-driven engagement (railing/parody)
rubrics_metrics.description: The distinguishing motivation is engagement "solely for the purpose of railing against or parodying" the media or person rather than fandom or constructive criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating online content or communities, assess whether activity centers on negative commentary/parody as primary aim; occasional criticism does not necessarily make one an anti-fan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavioural forms: hate-watching and snark
rubrics_metrics.description: Anti-fandom appears in many forms from hate-watching to snark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for behaviors such as intentionally watching to ridicule, producing snarky commentary, creating parody content, or systematically attending to a text/person to criticize rather than enjoy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group formation and anti-fan clubs/sites
rubrics_metrics.description: Large anti-fandoms commonly gather in groups, usually on forums and sites, to share their mutual aversion; these are coined anti-fan clubs and some are substantial enough to become anti-fan sites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Community presence (forums, sites, coordinated activity) signals organized anti-fandom; evaluate the scale, methods of coordination, and whether the community centers on negativity as identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community dynamics: 'haters attract haters' / reciprocity
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a saying that "haters attract haters", suggesting that individuals who express negativity or hostility may draw similar reactions from others. This is rooted in reciprocity, where negative energy or behavior can be mirrored and reciprocated by those who encounter it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how negativity propagates: whether hostile behavior recruits others or creates echo chambers; consider moderation, platform affordances, and feedback loops that sustain negativity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subtypes: anti-shipper
rubrics_metrics.description: Someone who opposes a ship (a romantic pairing between two characters) is called an anti-shipper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize specific sub-forms of anti-fandom (e.g., anti-shipping) that focus opposition on particular aspects of a text (relationships, characters) rather than the whole work or creator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmful or extreme outcomes (real-world harm, stalking, security concerns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Anti-fan activity can escalate to real-world harm: e.g., in 2006 an anti-fan of the K-pop duo TVXQ poisoned member Yunho with a super glue-laced drink. Such occurrences have resulted in an increase of security for celebrities in South Korea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating risk, note evidence of threats, stalking, violence, or coordinated harassment; distinguish rhetorical negativity from actions that create physical danger or criminal activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholarly focus: marginalization and identity-based discrediting
rubrics_metrics.description: Anti-fan studies focus on specific communities of practice and their relationship to media texts and fans actively marginalizing or discrediting other fans solely on basis of identity (sex, race, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Academic evaluation examines power, identity, and ethics: consider whether anti-fandom behavior targets marginalized groups, reproduces exclusionary norms, or intersects with broader social biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Related phenomena and overlap with other behaviours
rubrics_metrics.description: Anti-fandom overlaps with or is related to concepts such as cancel culture, cringe culture, cyberbullying, internet trolling, online shaming, sasaeng fan behaviour, stalking, fanaticism and celebrity worship syndrome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these related categories to contextualize anti-fan activity; overlap may indicate shared mechanisms (harassment, public shaming) and inform mitigations or interventions.
